extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, editors, and writers (including press officers and PR/marketing writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on structuring news stories (and related texts such as press releases) so the most important information appears first, with supporting/detail material following in descending importance. Emphasises the summary lead (BLUF), inclusion of the Five Ws and H, and techniques that make editing and reader comprehension easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise most substantial, interesting, important information at the top (inverted pyramid / BLUF)
rubrics_metrics.description: The widest part at the top represents the most substantial, interesting, and important information that the writer means to convey, illustrating that this kind of material should head the article. It is sometimes called a summary news lead style, or bottom line up front (BLUF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the key facts and takeaways in the opening sentences so readers immediately get the core story. This helps readers who stop reading early and is the fundamental organising principle of the inverted pyramid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the Five Ws and H in the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Who, when, where, why, what, and how are addressed in the first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure the lead answers the essential questions; a pyramid-conscious reporter might also move two additional critical details into the first two sentences (example: that the shot was to the head and was expected to prove fatal). Being specific in the lead improves clarity and news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange subsequent material in order of diminishing importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The tapering lower portion illustrates that other material should follow in order of diminishing importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the lead, present supporting facts, context, background, and lesser details in descending priority so that the story can be shortened from the bottom without losing essential information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate editing by 'cutting from the bottom'
rubrics_metrics.description: This system also means that information less vital to the reader's understanding comes later in the story, where it is easier to edit out for space or other reasons. This is called 'cutting from the bottom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure copy so sub-editors can shorten the story by removing trailing paragraphs without damaging the core message; keep expendable detail lower down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a hook/prologue when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The inverted pyramid may also include a 'hook' as a kind of prologue, typically a provocative quote, question, or image, to entice the reader into committing to reading the full story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A brief attention-grabbing element before the summary lead can draw readers in, but should not replace the essential summary facts that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: End with a 'kicker' or call to action in feature style
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than petering out, a story may end with a 'kicker'—a conclusion, perhaps call to action—which comes after the pyramid. This is particularly common in feature style articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For feature-like pieces or marketing/PR copy, consider adding a concluding payoff or call to action after the core inverted-pyramid content to leave readers with a memorable close.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'burying the lead'
rubrics_metrics.description: The opposite, the failure to mention the most important, interesting or attention-grabbing elements of a story in the opening paragraphs, is called burying the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not hide the story's central facts deeper in the text; ensure the lead carries the story's primary news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose alternative lead formats when they better serve the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Other styles are also used in news writing, including the 'anecdotal lead', which begins the story with an eye-catching tale or anecdote rather than the central facts; and the Q&A, or question-and-answer format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the inverted pyramid for clarity and skimmability, but use anecdotal leads, Q&A, or narrative when they better suit the story's goals, tone, or audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the inverted pyramid to related formats (blogs, editorials, press releases, marketing factsheets)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a common method for writing news stories and has wide adaptability to other kinds of texts, such as blogs, editorial columns and marketing factsheets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing press releases or marketing copy, use the inverted-pyramid approach to present the key message and facts first so journalists and busy readers can quickly grasp the news; follow with supporting details and boilerplate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design leads for reader behavior (readers can leave at any point and understand)
rubrics_metrics.description: This format is valued because readers can leave the story at any point and understand it, even if they do not have all the details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume many readers will skim or stop early; make the opening self-sufficient so the essential information is understood without the full article.
